description: Team Valore Astra is a London-based team for NASA Space Apps 2026. "Valore" means value and courage in Italian; "astra" means stars. We'll use NASA's open data to build something useful and try bold ideas. I'm a second-year computer science student into AI/ML, software and space. We're a relaxed, supportive team: learning and fun matter as much as winning.
summary:
Rotara helps farmers decide what to plant next as their climate shifts. 

A farmer drops a pin or types a postcode, picks the crop they grow now, and says what matters to them: saving water, building soil, adding nitrogen, fewer pests, or keeping changes small. Rotara compares 25 years of NASA POWER data for that field (temperature, rain and root-zone soil wetness), with GPM IMERG rain and SMAP soil moisture as independent checks, and shows what has changed. It then offers 3 crop rotations for the next 3 years: keep the current crop, mix in climate-suited crops, or build the soil with a cover crop. Each plan shows which priorities it meets, what to check first, the cited agronomy rule behind it, and what it does not know. 

In Norfolk, UK, yearly rain fell only 2% but summer rain fell 30%, a change that a yearly total hides. Rotara is free, needs no account and stores nothing. The farmer always decides.
details:
THE PROBLEM

A farm's yearly rain total can hide the change that matters. In Norfolk, UK, rain over the whole year fell only 2% (706 mm to 693 mm, 2001–2020 vs 2021–2025), but summer rain fell 30% (206 mm to 145 mm), right when crops need it most. Farmers need to see changes like this in their field and turn them into a rotation they can trust.

WHAT ROTARA DOES

1. Find the field: drop a pin on the map or type a postcode or village.

2. Pick the crop grown there now.

3. See what changed: compare recent years (2021–2025) with the usual (2001–2020) for temperature, yearly and seasonal rain, root-zone soil wetness, and climate risk level. The last 30 days add frosty nights, heat-stress days (30°C or more) and heavy rain days (20 mm or more).

4. Tell us about the farm: priorities (use less water, build organic matter, add nitrogen, stop soil washing away, fewer pests and diseases, feed for livestock, easy to sell, keep changes small), water, machinery, a buyer for a new crop, soil type and an optional soil-test figure.

5. Compare 3 plans for the next 3 years: keep the current crop, mix in climate-suited crops, or add a cover crop to build the soil. Each plan shows which priorities it matches, what to check first, why it was suggested, the cited evidence, what could go wrong and what was not checked.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python (FastAPI) backend reads NASA data and runs a rules engine. The engine scores climate risk using simple, documented thresholds (warmer by 0.5 °C or more; yearly or summer rain down 5% or more) and builds the 3 rotations from crop rules taken from published guidance, each with its source. For example, pulses such as field beans never appear twice in three years, because AHDB advises at least five years between pulse crops. The farmer's answers never change the science: they add notes to each plan and can mark one as the best fit. A Next.js website shows everything in plain words, including the source of every figure.

HONEST ABOUT LIMITS 

Every number is labelled as NASA data, calculated, or the farmer's input. Satellite data that NASA flags as low quality is not used: for our Nevada example farm, none of the 1,492 SMAP readings had recommended quality, so the app says so instead of showing them. A guide page explains NDVI, evapotranspiration, soil moisture anomalies, and satellite vs ground data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT 

A farmer gets a field-level picture in minutes, free, with no account. Nothing is stored after the session. The plans are meant to start a conversation with an agronomist, not replace one.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, pytest (133 backend tests), TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js, Mapbox GL JS and Mapbox geocoding, and Gemma 4 run locally through Ollama for the optional explain-the-plans chat. Hosted on Vercel and Render. Code: https://github.com/Valorz1/field-shift

USE OF AI

The crop plans come from a rules engine with cited sources, not from AI. An optional chat uses Gemma 4, running locally, to explain the existing plans in 1–2 lines; it does not create plans or change numbers, and it is not on the deployed site. During development the team used Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) for coding, testing, code review and research; Microsoft Copilot (Codex model) to build the deployment layer; ChatGPT (OpenAI) for text formatting and research; and Base44 for an early dashboard design prototype. The demo slides were generated with Canva's AI from our own outline, then checked and edited by the team. The demo video was made by the team from real recordings of the app, the NASA HLS satellite image and Pixabay music, with light AI help for editing; the voiceover is a team member. AI-assisted commits are marked as co-authored in the repository, and every AI-assisted change was reviewed by a team member, checked against its sources where it states a fact, and tested. Full statement: https://rotara-chi.vercel.app/about

More NASA data

- Crop greenness (NDVI) for the farmer's own field boundary from HLS and Landsat to spot stressed patches and check whether a plan is working.

- Water use (evapotranspiration) from ECOSTRESS and MODIS to put a real number on how much water each plan needs.

- SMAP Level 4 root-zone soil moisture, which fills the gaps where the satellite alone has too few reliable readings (like our Nevada farm).

- GRACE groundwater trends as context for farms that rely on irrigation.

- Seasonal outlooks from NASA's GEOS forecasts, so plans can look ahead as well as back.

Better plans

- Local soil data (pH, texture, organic carbon) from open soil maps, so the plans can start from the field's real soil.

- More crops and more regions, each with rules from local agricultural advice.

- A one-page plan summary the farmer can download and take to their adviser, still with nothing stored on our side.

Easier to use

- Draw the field boundary instead of a single pin.

- More languages and a version that works with a weak signal in the field.

- Open-source maps (MapLibre), so the site needs no paid map account.

Proving it works

- Test the plans with farmers and an agronomist in Norfolk and Nevada, and check the crop rules against local advice before any wider use.

Background research (11 pages, 30 references): https://github.com/Valorz1/field-shift/blob/main/docs/research.pdf

Slides: https://canva.link/um5s5uhjp8bd9gc
